## Introduction

This supplementary exercise is outside the timed programme and takes
about 15 minutes. You will generate a synthetic version of the
`HealthWellbeing` study summaries with *synthpop*, compare it with the
original, and run the same pooled analysis on both. By the end, you
should be able to explain what a synthetic dataset lets others test
and what it cannot establish.

Run the chunks in the **R Console** from the project root, in the
prepared environment, after preparing the dataset versions.
[Prepare the dataset versions](00_preparation.qmd#preparation-versions)

## Prepare the study summaries

We read the full 29-study dataset by its recorded pin version, so the
exercise starts from the same input as the workshop pipeline.

```{r health-extras-data, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
box::use(pins[board_folder, pin_read], utils[read.csv])

source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
workshop_dir <- workshop_output_dir()
versions <- read.csv(
  file.path(workshop_dir, "dataset-versions.csv"),
  colClasses = "character"
)
full_version <- versions$version[versions$scope == "all"]
stopifnot(length(full_version) == 1L)

data_board <- board_folder(
  file.path(workshop_dir, "data_store"),
  versioned = TRUE
)
health_full <- pin_read(
  data_board, "health_wellbeing", version = full_version
)
stopifnot(nrow(health_full) == 29L)

original <- data.frame(
  population = factor(health_full$population),
  z = atanh(health_full$cor),
  log_n = log(health_full$n)
)
```

`z` is the Fisher transformation of the correlation, and `log_n`
is the natural log of the study sample size. The example uses
study summaries and leaves out the original study labels and country
column.

## Generate synthetic study summaries

We use the CART synthesis method with seed 123, so the run can be
repeated in the same environment. We convert the generated values to
the original scales and give the new rows synthetic labels. The
generated sample sizes describe synthetic rows, not real studies.

```{r health-synthetic-data, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
box::use(synthpop[compare, syn])

synthetic <- syn(
  original,
  method = "cart",
  seed = 123,
  print.flag = FALSE
)

synthetic_data <- data.frame(
  author = sprintf("Synthetic %02d", seq_len(nrow(synthetic$syn))),
  cor = tanh(synthetic$syn$z),
  n = round(exp(synthetic$syn$log_n)),
  population = synthetic$syn$population
)
head(synthetic_data)
compare(synthetic, original)
```

Inspect the distributions of `population`, `z`, and `log_n`. The
comparison describes how closely the two tables resemble each other
on these variables. Similar distributions can coexist with
differences in the relationships between variables and in downstream
estimates. For the synthesis methods, see @nowok2016-synthpop and the
[synthpop documentation](https://www.synthpop.org.uk/).

## Try it yourself: pool both datasets

Run the workshop's random-effects model on the original and the
synthetic study summaries, and compare the pooled correlations.

```{r health-synthetic-pool, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
box::use(meta[metacor])

pool_correlations <- function(data) {
  model <- metacor(
    cor = cor,
    n = n,
    studlab = author,
    data = data,
    sm = "ZCOR",
    common = FALSE,
    random = TRUE,
    method.tau = "REML",
    method.random.ci = "HK"
  )
  c(
    studies = model$k,
    pooled_r = tanh(model$TE.random),
    ci_lower = tanh(model$lower.random),
    ci_upper = tanh(model$upper.random)
  )
}

round(
  rbind(
    original = pool_correlations(health_full),
    synthetic = pool_correlations(synthetic_data)
  ),
  3
)
```

The analysis code runs unchanged on the synthetic table, so a reader
without access to restricted originals could test that the workflow
works. The synthetic estimate is computed from generated rows. A close
match would not verify the original finding, and a difference would
not refute it.

## Limits on interpretation and sharing

Treat this as a public teaching example. Ordinary synthesis with
*synthpop* is not a differential privacy guarantee, and a distribution
comparison or utility score does not establish one. A privacy claim
requires a validated mechanism and privacy accounting
[@near2021-synthetic-data]. Synthetic data also does not confer
privacy protection on related models, evaluation results, or
metadata. Keep generated tables local until you have checked the
applicable release terms.

## Checkpoint {#synthetic-checkpoint}

-   You generated 29 synthetic study summaries with labelled synthetic
    rows and compared their distributions with the original.
-   You ran the same pooled analysis on both tables and can explain
    why a matching estimate would not verify the original finding.
-   You can explain why synthetic data is not, by itself, a privacy
    guarantee.
